claims.text: The degree of short-range chemical ordering governs toughness retention under high-loading conditions.
Short-range chemical ordering affects toughness by modulating local energy barriers for dislocation and twin interactions at the crack tip.
Increasing SRO through controlled heat treatment enhances crack-tip blunting and delays crack propagation.
The proposed initial material is a near-equimolar, single-phase or dual-phase HEA such as CoCrFeMnNi.
The initial material has a low-to-moderate level of SRO.
Varying heat-treatment soak temperature and duration can progressively increase SRO without changing the overall phase composition.
The comparison should be conducted at a constant high strain rate of approximately 10^6 per second and at operationally relevant temperatures.
SRO consists of ordering in near-neighbor atomic arrangements and can be quantified using APT or HRSTEM.
Enhanced SRO increases the ruggedness of the local energy landscape and raises barriers to dislocation activity.
Enhanced SRO promotes favorable dislocation-twin or dislocation-phase-boundary coupling near a crack tip.
The SRO-induced interactions redistribute stress and facilitate crack blunting.
Lower SRO produces less impeded dislocation motion.
Less impeded dislocation motion is less effective at arresting crack propagation.
Samples with higher SRO will have greater fracture toughness, higher crack-initiation energy, more ductile fracture morphology, and delayed crack propagation relative to the lower-SRO baseline.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to near-equimolar single-phase or dual-phase HEAs under high-strain-rate, moderate-to-high-temperature conditions.
Significant phase transformations or conditions outside the range of SRO-stabilized microstructures may limit the hypothesis.
Twinning and phase transformations may concurrently affect toughness and confound attribution to SRO.
Failure of higher-SRO specimens to show a statistically significant toughness improvement, or toughness varying independently of SRO, would falsify the hypothesis.
